overview.text: The Southern California Rapid Transit District and the federal Urban Mass Transportation Administration are studying eleven ways to improve transit in a 55-square-mile 'Regional Core' of central Los Angeles — the corridor running from downtown through Wilshire Boulevard to Hollywood and North Hollywood — home to about 600,000 residents and 542,000 jobs. The choices range from an 18-mile underground rail line down to reserved bus lanes on existing streets, plus a 'no build' baseline; capital costs run from about $196 million to about $2.02 billion. The most extensive rail option (Alternative II, an 18-mile Wilshire–Fairfax–North Hollywood subway) would carry the most riders and cut about 100,000 auto trips and 710,000 vehicle miles per day compared with no build, but building elevated 'aerial' guideways would displace hundreds of buildings, cast shadows on parks and historic buildings, and risk damage to fossil and archaeological finds near the La Brea Tar Pits, while surface bus-lane options would clog traffic and eliminate curb parking on Wilshire and La Brea. After four rounds of over 30 community meetings, participants tended to favor rail over bus but voiced strong concerns about earthquake risk, construction disruption (especially cut-and-cover subway digging), and effects on businesses.

project_description.text: The Southern California Rapid Transit District (SCRTD) and the federal Urban Mass Transportation Administration are evaluating eleven ways to improve transit in a 55-square-mile triangular 'Regional Core' of central Los Angeles, bounded roughly by Robertson Boulevard, Burbank Boulevard, the Hollywood Freeway/Sunset Boulevard/Alameda Street, and the Santa Monica Freeway. Five 'Rail Rapid Transit/Bus' options pair an 8- to 18-mile rail line (built either as a bored subway or on elevated 'aerial' guideway) with feeder buses, running from downtown Union Station along Wilshire toward Hollywood and North Hollywood; five all-bus options range from an elevated busway to reserved lanes on existing streets; and one 'Null' option keeps existing service. This project is Element IV of a four-part Regional Transit Development Program that also includes bus upgrades, freeway bus/carpool lanes, and a Downtown People Mover; after public hearings, the SCRTD Board and UMTA will pick one alternative as the project.

affected_community.text: The Regional Core holds about 599,000 residents (1975) and 542,000 jobs (1970) across six community plan areas — Central City, Westlake, Wilshire, Hollywood, Sherman Oaks–Studio City, and North Hollywood — with an average density of 10,776 residents per square mile. Roughly 41.7% of residents are minorities, and the Westlake–Central City median household income of $9,518 is about 32% below the citywide $14,030; transit-dependent groups include about 107,917 residents age 65+, 90,020 under 16, 3,400 handicapped persons, and 85,883 households without autos. The corridor contains ethnic communities like Chinatown and Little Tokyo, cultural sites like the Music Center and Hollywood Bowl, 265 identified cultural-historic resources, nineteen educational institutions, eight major medical facilities (Good Samaritan, Kaiser, Children's, Hollywood Presbyterian, and others), and ten major retail centers; Hancock Park Elementary School would sit within 100 feet of the Alternative II route.

alternatives_overview.text: Eleven options are compared. Rail/Bus Alternatives I–V are heavy-rail lines of 8 to 18 miles, all sharing a downtown alignment from Union Station south under Broadway and west from 7th Street, then diverging along Wilshire via La Brea (I), Fairfax (II), Vermont (III), a shorter version ending near the Hollywood Bowl (IV), or an 8-mile Wilshire-to-Fairfax stub (V); each can be built as bored subway or aerial guideway. Alternative VI is a 16-mile elevated 'aerial busway' on Alternative I's route; Alternatives VII and IX put exclusive median or curb bus lanes on Wilshire and La Brea; Alternative VIII is a reversible peak-period median bus lane on 8th and Olympic; Alternative X is a low-cost Transportation Systems Management package (bus rerouting and added frequency without new infrastructure); Alternative XI is the no-build baseline. Rail would run 24 hours, 7 days a week, with 3.5–4.5 minute peak headways, 6-car trains carrying up to 990 passengers, and average speeds of 35–40 mph; total escalated capital costs range from about $196 million (Alt. XI) to about $2.02 billion (Alt. II), and All-Bus options could be built in five years versus seven to eight for rail or the aerial busway.

environmental_impact.text: Rail alternatives would draw 574,000–642,000 daily riders (versus 403,000 today), and Alternative II would cut roughly 100,000 daily auto trips and 710,000 vehicle miles compared with no build; even so, auto trips in the Regional Core still grow 12% from 1977 to 1990 under the best alternative versus 16% under Null. Building elevated 'aerial' guideways would displace between 78 structures (Alt. V) and 723 structures (Alt. II) and could bisect MacArthur Park (Alts. I–V) and Barnsdall Park (Alt. III), while surface bus-lane Alternatives VII, VIII, and IX would cause severe traffic congestion by removing traffic lanes, closing minor cross streets, and eliminating curb parking on Wilshire and La Brea. Deep bored subway tunnels are judged safer in earthquakes than surface or aerial structures — the maximum credible earthquake (the worst quake considered plausible) is Magnitude 8.5 on the San Andreas Fault and Magnitude 7.0–7.5 on the Newport-Inglewood Fault two miles from the Starter Line, and 22,000 pre-1933 substandard brick buildings could drop debris on aerial structures. Tunneling near the La Brea Tar Pits could damage fossils and artifacts (well-preserved material has been found to nearly 60 feet deep, including the ~9,000-year-old 'La Brea woman') and produce tar, oil, and gas seeps for about 2.5 miles between Highland and Beverly, plus up to 600 gallons per minute of groundwater inflow under the Santa Monica Mountains. Regional air-quality gains from Alternative II are small (about 0.4 tons/day reactive hydrocarbons, 0.6 tons/day nitrogen oxides, and 3.4 tons/day carbon monoxide, roughly 0.1% of regional emissions), and Rail Alternatives I–V would save 29,000–44,000 equivalent barrels of oil per year in 1990 while All-Bus VII–X would use 28,000–39,000 more.

public_response.text: Over 14 months, SCRTD staff completed four rounds of more than 30 community and organization meetings, publicized through newspapers, radio, TV, bus notices, and mailings, and briefed the Los Angeles City Council's Transportation Committee and the LA County Transportation Commission's Citizens Advisory Committee. Participation reached corridor residents, out-of-corridor residents, affected businesses, municipalities, and transit dependents, plus regionwide groups including the League of Women Voters, Sierra Club, Urban League, LACEA, Building Industry Associates, and the Los Angeles NAACP. Key concerns raised by participants included costs and funding sources (with property taxes considered too high to use), earthquake dangers of a subway, adamant opposition to cut-and-cover subway construction, and worry that exclusive bus lanes would harm businesses along Wilshire; by the second round, participants generally favored rail over bus while viewing improved bus service as vital, and Hollywood community groups pressed for locating the Hollywood station at Cahuenga and Hollywood Boulevards. Historically, an 89-mile system proposed to voters in 1968 did not win approval and a 1974 proposal was defeated 47%–53% (though the City of Los Angeles voted yes), but in June 1974 over 60% of LA County voters approved Proposition 5, permitting motor vehicle revenues to be used for fixed-guideway transit but not buses.

summary_of_interest.claim: Tunneling near the La Brea Tar Pits could damage fossils and human artifacts preserved to nearly 60 feet deep, including the roughly 9,000-year-old 'La Brea woman,' and would encounter tar, oil, and gas seeps for about 2.5 miles between Highland and Beverly.
summary_of_interest.evidence_quote: Well-preserved floral and faunal materials have been recovered from the surface to a depth of nearly 60 feet in selected areas.
summary_of_interest.why_notable: Paleontological damage risk from active asphalt seeps along a subway route is an atypical impact category for a transit EIS and is site-specific to this Los Angeles corridor.

evidence.quote: Well-preserved floral and faunal materials have been recovered from the surface to a depth of nearly 60 feet in selected areas.

summary_of_interest.claim: The Los Angeles Police Department and SCRTD produced sharply conflicting transit-policing estimates — LAPD proposed 195 sworn officers for the 18-mile Alternative II while SCRTD estimated 45 — and the document adopts SCRTD's lower figure by citing Chicago's staffing ratio.
summary_of_interest.evidence_quote: Based on its judgment, the Los Angeles City Police Department estimates that it would require 195 sworn personnel to provide adequate police services for Alternative II.
summary_of_interest.why_notable: The document openly rejects the local police department's staffing estimate in favor of the transit district's, embedding a more than fourfold agency disagreement directly into the cost analysis.

evidence.quote: Based on its judgment, the Los Angeles City Police Department estimates that it would require 195 sworn personnel to provide adequate police services for Alternative II.

summary_of_interest.claim: Aerial guideway construction for Alternative II would displace 723 structures, and about 22,000 pre-1933 substandard brick buildings in the region could shed debris onto elevated structures during a major earthquake.
summary_of_interest.evidence_quote: The cut and cover and aerial configurations would cause considerable displacement of residences and commercial building, (from 78 for Alternative V to 723 for Alternative II).
summary_of_interest.why_notable: Displacement of over 700 buildings for a single alignment variant, combined with a documented risk that thousands of surrounding unreinforced brick buildings could collapse onto the guideway, is an unusually large combined impact.

evidence.quote: The cut and cover and aerial configurations would cause considerable displacement of residences and commercial building, (from 78 for Alternative V to 723 for Alternative II).

summary_of_interest.claim: The document treats a modeled 8-hour carbon monoxide concentration of 9.9 ppm at Lankershim and Chandler as exceeding the federal 9 ppm standard on occasion, even after the transit improvements.
summary_of_interest.evidence_quote: The standard for the Federal Government is 9 ppm for 8 hours and the 9.9 reasonable worst case sample may exceed this standard on occasion.
summary_of_interest.why_notable: The EIS acknowledges a modeled violation of a federal air quality standard at a proposed station area rather than claiming full compliance, which is unusual for a project justified partly on air quality grounds.

evidence.quote: The standard for the Federal Government is 9 ppm for 8 hours and the 9.9 reasonable worst case sample may exceed this standard on occasion.
